record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: Against an adversarial server, how can one construct efficient and robust secure aggregation that handles semi-honest setup assumptions, per-round aggregate leakage, sparse vectors, client input well-formedness, and client dropouts at large scale?

evidence.quote: how to construct an efficient and robust secure aggregation protocol

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a distributed computation setting with a central server S and a large set of clients C = {1, ..., n}, where each client i holds a private input vector x_i ∈ R^d (possibly sparse). A secure aggregation protocol is an interactive cryptographic protocol that allows S to learn the sum y = Σ_{i ∈ A} x_i over the set A ⊆ C of clients that successfully complete the protocol, while revealing no additional information about any individual x_i beyond what is implied by y and the adversary's view.

Assume the following adversarial model:
(a) The server S may be malicious (i.e., may deviate arbitrarily from the protocol), while a subset of clients may also be corrupted and colluding with S.
(b) The trusted-setup phase (e.g., distribution of cryptographic keys, public parameters) is only semi-honest: parties follow it honestly but the transcript may later leak to the adversary.
(c) The server obtains the aggregate output y in each round, and these per-round aggregates are considered acceptable leakage.
(d) Clients may drop out at arbitrary points during protocol execution, including adaptively.
(e) Inputs x_i are typically high-dimensional and sparse, and the protocol must enforce well-formedness of inputs (e.g., bounded norm, bounded sparsity, integer-valued in a prescribed range) so that malicious clients cannot poison the aggregate by submitting out-of-range vectors.

Design a secure aggregation protocol that simultaneously achieves the following:
1. Correctness: when honest parties follow the protocol, S obtains Σ_{i ∈ A} x_i for the set A of non-dropout honest clients.
2. Privacy against a malicious server colluding with a constant fraction of malicious clients, with security reducing only to semi-honest assumptions on the setup phase, and allowing only the per-round aggregate as leakage.
3. Robustness to an arbitrary (adaptive) pattern of client dropouts among the n clients, with output still correctly representing the sum of the surviving honest clients' inputs.
4. Verifiable input well-formedness: any contribution from a malicious client that does not lie in a prescribed admissible set (e.g., bounded ℓ∞- or ℓ2-norm, prescribed sparsity, prescribed quantization) is rejected.
5. Efficiency: per-client communication and computation, and server computation, scale at most polylogarithmically in n and quasi-linearly in the effective (sparse) input size, so that the protocol is practical for n on the order of 10^6 or more.

Provide such a protocol together with a proof of its security and complexity, or prove an impossibility/lower bound showing that no protocol can simultaneously achieve all of (1)–(5).
artifact.status_search_result: Secure aggregation against a malicious server with simultaneous handling of dropouts, sparse inputs, input well-formedness, and large-scale efficiency remains an active research area. Partial progress has been made (e.g., RoFL for input constraints, ACORN, Flamingo, SecAgg+, EIFFeL for malicious-server settings), but no single protocol has been shown to achieve all listed desiderata at the scale and efficiency demanded; the problem is generally regarded as still open.

status_evidence.title: Flamingo: Multi-Round Single-Server Secure Aggregation with Applications to Private Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Flamingo addresses multi-round secure aggregation with dropouts but with limited malicious-server guarantees and not full input well-formedness for sparse vectors.
status_evidence.claim: State-of-the-art secure aggregation protocols address subsets but not all of the listed requirements simultaneously.

status_evidence.title: EIFFeL: Ensuring Integrity for Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: EIFFeL provides input well-formedness checks for secure aggregation but with substantial overheads compared to baseline secure aggregation.
status_evidence.claim: Input-validation extensions of secure aggregation incur significant efficiency costs, indicating the combined problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: RoFL: Robustness of Secure Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: RoFL enforces norm bounds on client updates within secure aggregation but does not address fully malicious server with all listed properties.
status_evidence.claim: No known protocol simultaneously achieves all of malicious-server security, dropout robustness, sparsity, input validation, and polylog efficiency.
